newsitem.title: UK: UK MPs look at improving legislative procedures.
newsitem.headline: UK MPs look at improving legislative procedures.

text.p: Members of parliament on Tuesday gingerly proposed ways of improving the way the House of Commons scrutinise legislation in line with the new Labour government's determination to modernise British politics.
In a progress report, the newly established Select Committee on Modernisation of the House of Commons issued a series of recommendations to make the legislative process more effective.
In a symbolic change, the all-party panel also proposed changes to the daily House of Commons Order Paper, which it called very difficult to understand.

When parliament reconvenes on October 27 after the summer recess starting on Thursday, the Order Paper will be replaced by a "Daily Agenda", also available on the Internet, setting out the expected business and timetable for the day.
"The time is ripe for change," Ann Taylor, leader of the House of Commons and chairman of the committee, said.

"Members of the House want to see a more effective legislature, more input into the legislative process and be able to use their time more constructively, and I believe that these recommendations will help achieve this," she added.
-- Programming the passage of legislation to provide an alternative to the controversial practice of the government "guillotine" to cut short the time available for debate.
MPs recommend a more open and formal approach to programming bills, with a Standing Committee empowered to decide a timetable for the legislation being considered.

"It is not only new Members (of Parliament) who find the traditional approach unsatisfactory and in some respects incomprehensible. There are many Members with long experience who are thoroughly dissatisfied with the existing approach to this issue," the report said.

"We believe that the advent of a new parliament with so many new Members represents a real opportunity to break away from this approach and to try to create a new system which will benefit everyone," it added.

-- Increased opportunities for pre-legislative scrutiny and consultation. The government is already committed to publishing seven bills in draft, some of which could be examined in committee, the report said.
-- All committees of the House of Commons should be able to sit during recesses.
-- More flexibility in the parliamentary cycle to allow, in certain circumstances, bills to be carried over from one session of parliament to the next. This is currently not possible.
